column3: It shares the language of sending down, but concerns the divided recipients rather than authority for association.

It challenges whether alleged partners can benefit or harm and whether they create like God, directly testing the association asserted in the focus.
It demands that alleged partners show what they created or their share in the heavens, an explicit evidentiary test of their standing.
It asks what the alleged partners created, whether they share in the heavens, or possess a book as authorization.
It condemns calling another god with God while having no proof for the claim, directly parallel to the focus.

It concedes that God created the heavens and earth, then exposes the inability of other protectors to remove or withhold what God decrees.
It denies that God has a partner in dominion, stating the sovereignty premise that makes the focus's association untenable.

It identifies making the jinn partners with God as an invented claim contrary to His unique creative status.
It asks whether any alleged partner guides to truth, extending the focus's test from claimed speech to actual divine function.
It identifies following conjecture as insufficient for truth, helping explain the unsupported character of the association in the focus.
It depicts the separation of worshippers from their alleged partners and the partners' denial of the worship.
It describes worship of those who control no provision from heaven or earth, contrasting them with the source of provision.
It states that beings invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, directly weakening claims to partnership.

It asks whether people associate beings that create nothing and are themselves created, a direct capacity test.
It states that those called besides God cannot help their worshippers or themselves, clarifying their lack of agency.
It says those invoked besides God are not truly partners and that their followers only pursue conjecture.
It describes making rivals for God in order to lead from His path, showing the practical effect of association.
It says those invoked besides God cannot remove or alter harm, testing their asserted divine role.
It identifies taking gods besides God in hope of honor, clarifying a motive behind unsupported association.
It says the alleged gods will deny their worship and become opponents, exposing the collapse of the claimed relationship.
It confines deity to God alone, whose knowledge encompasses all things, supporting the focus's exclusive divine standing.
It argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would produce corruption, giving a rational refutation of divided divinity.
It asks whether they have taken gods from the earth and demands their proof, closely matching the focus's challenge.
It describes invoking what neither harms nor benefits, directly questioning the agency assigned to others besides God.
It affirms God as the true reality and others invoked besides Him as falsehood, framing the focus's verdict.
It begins a sequence asking who owns the earth and its inhabitants, testing claims of shared divine possession.
It asks who holds sovereignty over everything and protects without needing protection, directly excluding equal partners.
It rejects any additional god by showing that each would take its creation and seek dominance over the others.
It describes alleged gods that neither create, control death, nor control life or resurrection, directly refuting divine partnership.
It says idols cannot provide provision and directs seekers to God for provision, supporting the focus's provision-based challenge.

It asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, directly denying a rival source of provision.

It denies that those gods can help, despite being an assembled host for their worshippers.
It asks whether false gods are desired besides God, confronting the arbitrariness of the association.

Its parable of one servant with competing masters contrasts divided allegiance with exclusive devotion to one master.
It asks where the partners besides God are, bringing the focus's claim into an eschatological accounting.
It asks whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were instituted for worship, testing the claim against revelation.
